inline.s: Q: When reciting the Buddha’s name with the ten recitations and counting, I recite two phrases at a time, taking two phrases as one group, and count five times to make ten phrases. As I recite, I count each group clearly, so that counting is easy and the mind is well gathered in. May I recite in this way?
A: Of course you may. It is easy and it gathers in the mind — this is very good.
Q: How should one train in “ten recitations continuing without interruption, so that practice becomes second nature”?

A: This may be done in two ways. On the one hand, recite ten phrases after ten phrases without stopping, making it ever more familiar until it becomes utterly proficient. On the other hand, cultivate the power of recollecting the Buddha, making it focused, continuous, and enduring. The method is this: raise one recitation of the Buddha’s name, and with it — focused, fine and unbroken, as a child longs for its mother — recollect Amitābha Buddha (
the Buddha’s light shines upon body and mind, and one receives great empowerment

). Then, when a deluded thought is about to arise, raise the name once more, and with it recollect Amitābha Buddha, focused, fine and unbroken, as a child longs for its mother; and so continue. Let no deluded thought intrude between the two phrases, and the longer the interval between them the better. As days pass and the work deepens, then not only will ten recitations continue without interruption, but a hundred recitations, a thousand recitations, will continue without interruption — at all times continuing without interruption.

[Ten recitations continuing without interruption] In the course of reciting ten phrases of the Buddha’s name, thought of the Buddha follows thought of the Buddha without interruption, with no deluded thought mixed in — that is, ten phrases without confusion. And ten recitations continuing without interruption at the moment of death is of the utmost importance! Master Daochuo, in the Compendium of Peace and Bliss (Anle Ji), explains the meaning of the eighteenth vow:

“If there be living beings who, though they have committed evil all their lives, at the moment of death recite my name ten times without interruption, and are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”

[Practice becomes second nature] Through constant repeated practice, ten recitations continuing without interruption becomes instinctive. [As a child longs for its mother, so recollect Amitābha Buddha] Master Yinguang says in his Praise of Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta:
“As a child recalls its mother, so recall the World-Honored One
(Amitābha Buddha)

, and straightaway one receives grace. When the mind of the aspirant and the fruit of enlightenment accord, at once one returns to the source and goes back to the origin, and the wonder of gathering in all six faculties cannot be spoken.”
[The Buddha’s light shines upon body and mind, and one receives great empowerment] The Sutra of Immeasurable Life says:

“If there be living beings who encounter this light, the three defilements are extinguished, body and mind become gentle, they rejoice and leap for joy, and the mind of goodness arises in them. If they are in the places of extreme suffering of the three paths, then seeing this radiance they all find repose and are freed from affliction. After death they all receive liberation.”

[The three defilements] Another name for the three poisons, namely greed, anger, and delusion. [The three paths] The path of fire, the path of knives, and the path of blood, that is, the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals of the three evil destinies — places produced by evil karma of body, mouth, and mind. (1) The path of fire, that is, the hell realm, where beings are constantly tormented by cauldrons of boiling water and furnaces of burning charcoal, and so it is called the path of fire. (2) The path of knives, that is, the realm of hungry ghosts, where beings constantly suffer from being driven and threatened with knives and staves, and so it is called the path of knives. (3) The path of blood, that is, the animal realm, where the strong overpower the weak and devour one another, drinking blood and eating flesh, and so it is called the path of blood.

Once you are undisturbed through ten phrases, you may begin to train in being undisturbed through a hundred. Achieve a hundred recitations of the Buddha’s name into which water cannot be poured and wind cannot blow — like a wall of silver and a rampart of iron. At that point the hundred recitations of the Buddha’s name are like the Tai’e sword, like a great wheel of fire — sharp instruments for subduing afflictions. No sooner does the wind of circumstances rise than you immediately hold it down with a hundred recitations of the Buddha’s name. If that still does not work, recite another hundred, and so on, until the Buddha’s name prevails over the afflictions. When the work is deep, the moment the wind of circumstances blows, the Buddha’s name arises — not a drop leaks away — and the afflictions are naturally subdued. Zhongfeng’s Threefold Recitation says:
“Like the Tai’e sword, laid across the carriage rail; like a great wheel of fire, with blazing flames leaping up. All things that touch it are scorched, all things that meet it are wounded.”

To recite a hundred phrases of the Buddha’s name takes about a minute and a half. Each day, besides the regular period of Buddha-recitation, you must seize every available moment to recite one “hundred phrases of the Buddha’s name (ten sets of ten)” with full attention. Practice it as much as you can, and practice it until you are utterly proficient, so that at any time and in any place you can recite the whole run through without deluded thinking. Remember: one share of cultivation, one share of harvest; the work never betrays a willing heart, and you are certain to succeed!
Q: How does one count a hundred phrases?

A: The counting may be done on the fingers: with the left hand, bend one finger for every ten phrases recited; when all five fingers are bent, then extend one finger for every ten phrases; when all five fingers are extended, one hundred phrases have been recited.
Q: How does one train in “not being confused through a hundred phrases”?

A: For every hundred phrases recited, review how those hundred were recited. Generally there are three cases: first, no deluded thoughts at all; second, deluded thoughts are present but do not become sustained thinking; third, deluded thoughts arise and continue until they become sustained thinking. Then, according to the case, identify what should be maintained and what needs improvement, and decide how the next hundred phrases are to be recited. Having recited another hundred phrases, review in the same way and again decide how the next hundred are to be recited; and so continue. Training in this way is not only interesting, it brings rapid progress. In addition, if while reciting the Buddha’s name you find that some matter keeps circling in your mind, then pause and take up the prajñā contemplation, think it through thoroughly, and then hold it down with the Buddha’s name. Remember: for every hundred phrases you recite, you must have a clear idea of how those hundred phrases were recited.

You may also train in “not being confused through a hundred phrases” in this way: after every ten phrases, check whether you have fallen into deluded thinking. If you are indulging in deluded thinking, look at what the deluded thinking is about — what is it that tugs at your mind? — so that you may apply the remedy to the disease. Persevere in this without letting up, and as days pass and the work deepens, the ten sets of the Buddha’s name (ten phrases each) will of themselves join into one continuous whole.

Q: Generally speaking, I can subdue afflictions with the Buddha’s name. But when I meet with matters that pierce the heart or touch me personally, I cannot help but indulge in deluded thinking. What should I do?

A: This is precisely a good opportunity to advance on the path. In the third stage of the course of the “Online Buddhist Academy of Practice According to the Teaching,” “Prajnā Smashing Delusion,” we studied four sutras: the Diamond Sutra, the Heart Sutra, the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, and the Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury; and in the fourth stage, “The Pure Land as Home,” the Treatise on Buddha-Recitation and the Essentials of Chan and Pure Land. Now is exactly the time to study these matters that pierce the heart and touch you personally in a living way, and to see through them intimately. Master Hanshan says in his Song of Wasted Leisure:

“Reciting sutras is easy, understanding them hard; to recite with the mouth and not understand is always idle. To understand and not practice is wasted effort; a thousand volumes a day are likewise vain.”

Therefore, in studying the sutras and treatises one must not only recite and understand them, but still more practice according to them — practice as taught — before one can gain real benefit. In doing the work, you must especially test yourself at the two extremes of gain and loss, honor and disgrace, sorrow and joy, suffering and happiness. Once you have seen through them, hold down these deluded thoughts with the Buddha’s name, and you will have taken another great step forward on the bodhi path.
Q: Letting go is the hardest thing. What method should be used to counter it?
A: The skill of not being confused through a hundred phrases is exactly what is needed here. Mr. Liu Zhuyuan taught:

“Know that when you cannot let go, recite the Buddha’s name single-mindedly, and you will be able to let go. The Pure Land teaching’s parable of the clear pearl purifying muddy water is just this. If the mind scatters, counter it with the Buddha’s name, and after a long time it will settle of itself. In learning any dharma, who does not use bitter effort? If without effort one could suddenly let go, what need would there be to learn?”
(Letters of Mr. Liu Zhuyuan) Pay special attention to the word “counter” — this is the key to doing the work.

Once you are undisturbed through a hundred phrases, train further, joining the hundreds into a thousand and achieving being undisturbed through a thousand phrases. The method is this: after every hundred phrases, check whether you have fallen into deluded thinking?

If you are indulging in deluded thinking, look at what the deluded thinking is about — what is it that tugs at your mind? — so that you may apply the remedy to the disease. Persevere in this without letting up,

and as days pass and the work deepens, ten stretches of the Buddha’s name (each of a hundred phrases) will of themselves join into one continuous whole, forming a prairie fire, and the gnats will have nowhere to hide.

The counting may be done on the fingers: with the left hand, bend one finger for every ten phrases recited; when all five fingers are bent, extend one finger for every ten phrases; when all five are extended, one hundred phrases have been recited. Then add the right hand: for every hundred phrases, bend or extend one finger; when the five fingers of the right hand have been bent and extended through, that is one thousand phrases.

Or you may count each hundred phrases by bending and extending the five fingers of the left hand, and for every hundred counted, silently note a number in the mind: for example, 1 means one hundred phrases, 2 means two hundred phrases, and when you reach 10, that is a thousand phrases.
Q: Reciting the Buddha’s name in this way, the left hand must bend and extend to count and the mind must silently note numbers — is this not a distraction?

A: This is an expedient preliminary for attaining one mind undisturbed at all times. Since the left hand must count the tens and the mind must count the hundreds, it is not easy to fall into deluded thinking; not only is the Buddha’s name held “clear and distinct, neither dull nor scattered,” but the power of the mind grows ever more concentrated and the power of awareness steadily increases, laying a good foundation for being undisturbed at all times. Of course, you may also use your left hand
to count a hundred phrases by bending and extending all five fingers
, and with each hundred phrases of the Buddha’s name, press your right finger on the recitation counter.

Since beginningless kalpas living beings have been controlled by chattering deluded thoughts, suffering beyond words and moreover creating karma and reaping its retribution. Now that you have the skill of being undisturbed through a thousand phrases, you must free yourself from this control, subdue the afflictions, and take charge of your own mind. Therefore, as soon as you discover that you are controlled by chattering deluded thoughts, drifting helplessly from one thing to the next in idle imagining, you must at once raise the Buddha’s name and cut it off, until the Buddha’s name prevails over the afflictions. You must keep a state of alertness at all times and constantly, repeatedly cut off the chattering idle imaginings. When the work is familiar, the moment a deluded thought arises you will notice it at once, and at once raise the Buddha’s name to cut it off.
Generally speaking, one passes through a process like this:
1. A deluded thought comes, and only after indulging in it for a while do you notice. And when you raise the Buddha’s name to cut it off, it takes some effort.
2. A deluded thought comes, and after a brief moment of deluded thinking you notice it, and can raise the Buddha’s name to cut it off at once.
3. A deluded thought comes, and you notice it immediately, and at once raise the Buddha’s name to cut it off.

So long as you persevere without letting up, you will certainly arrive at this: the moment a thought arises, you are aware; and the moment you are aware, it is cut off. In this way the afflictions are held down.

Q: My way of training is to alternate: recite a thousand phrases of the Buddha’s name, then sit in stillness for a quarter of an hour. In the stillness I “am aware of the mind’s thoughts” (see the chapter “Awareness of Thoughts” in the Preliminary Practices section). May I do this?
A: This is a good method.
[Sitting in stillness] Sitting quietly with the mind collected.
Q: The Pure Land school cultivates the pure mind. May I ask: what is the pure mind?
A: The pure mind is the mind free of afflictions. The Diamond Sutra says:

“All bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should thus give rise to the pure mind; they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, nor should they give rise to a mind dwelling on sound, scent, taste, touch, or dharmas.”
A Buddha-reciter turns the defiled mind into the pure mind by reciting the Buddha’s name. Master Hanshan says:

“What is called the root of birth and death is none other than the various deluded thoughts of our daily use — the afflictions and karma of self and others, hate and love, greed, anger, and delusion, and so on. If even a single thread of these is not cut, it is the root of birth and death. ... Now if one can in truth take the mind of deluded thought and turn it into Buddha-recitation, then thought after thought one cuts off afflictions. If thought after thought one can cut off afflictions, then thought after thought one leaves birth and death behind. If this one thought is undisturbed, then at the approach of death evil karma is extinguished, the realm of the Buddha appears before one, and with a single thought one follows the Buddha to rebirth in the Pure Land, forever transcending birth and death and ascending to the stage of non-retrogression.”
(Dream Journey Collection · Reply to Wang Yufan)

To be undisturbed at all times, you must first keep the Buddha’s name unbroken at all times — what is called “before attaining non-disturbance, first make it unbroken.” For this you must let go of the myriad conditions, recite the Buddha’s name single-mindedly, not sparing day or night, practicing finely and closely (“close practice” means keeping the work fine and unbroken). When working, concentrate on your work; at all other times, keep the Buddha’s name unbroken in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. On weekends and holidays, keep the Buddha’s name unbroken the whole time. Persevere without letting up until it becomes a fixed rule and a formed habit. At all times remind and warn yourself: is there anything more important than escaping birth and death? Master Yinguang says:

“Walking, standing, sitting, lying; dressing, eating; from morning to night and from night to morning — let one phrase of the Buddha’s name never be interrupted. Recite it softly, or recite it silently; apart from Buddha-recitation, give rise to no other thought. If a deluded thought should arise, it must be made to perish on the spot.”
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang · Letter in Reply to Layman Ye Fubei, First)

As the saying goes: the fist never leaves the hand, the song never leaves the mouth. If people must strive so hard merely to master a skill, can we who wish to escape birth and death be unable even to keep the Buddha’s name unbroken? What in the world is accomplished at a single stroke without bitter effort? How much more so for cultivation that leaves the three realms! In truth, cultivation is great joy within hardship, and when the hardship is exhausted the sweetness comes. When you recite the Buddha’s name until thought after thought recites the Buddha and thought after thought is undimmed, the joy within this is joy beyond bearing. When you recite the Buddha’s name until you are born by transformation in the lotus and merge into the present moment, and the shadow of death no longer shrouds you, how can the serenity and certainty in your heart be put into words? Of this Master Yinguang says:

“The moment the Buddha’s name is raised, deluded thoughts all vanish; coolness pervades the body, and joy fills the breast. It is just like sweet dew poured over the crown, like ghee anointing the heart. Its joy cannot be described.”
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang · Tracing the Elephant of Buddha-Recitation Samādhi)

[Sweet dew] In Sanskrit amṛta, translated as sweet dew. Its taste is sweet as honey; it is the food of gods and humans. The Words and Phrases of the Golden Light says: “Sweet dew is the deathless medicine of the gods; whoever eats it lives long, his body is at peace, his strength is great, and his body shines.” Here sweet dew is a figure for the water of wisdom. [Anointing the crown] “Anoint” means the great compassion that protects and remembers; “crown” means the supreme fruit of Buddhahood: it means that all Buddhas anoint one with the water of wisdom, enabling one’s merits to be perfected. [Ghee] Butter refined through many stages, first among flavors; a figure for the supreme vehicle of the Buddha-Dharma.

Moreover, people under the endless entanglement of problems are burdened with heavy pressure and worn out in body and mind; yet almost all these problems are invented by their own thinking (many have not even recognized this much). For a cultivator, the single item of a pure mind already makes the quality of life far higher than that of ordinary people, not to speak of the fact that their karmic causes and retributions are as far apart as heaven and earth.

Karmic obstacles are the various hindrances of this life brought about by the various evil karma created in former lives, so that whatever one does goes contrary to one’s wishes. So people often ask: how does one dissolve karmic obstacles? Bear this firmly in mind: when a deluded thought arises, it is karma binding the mind; to replace it with the Buddha’s name — this is the mind turning karma. Do this continuously at all times and in all places, and naturally karma will dissolve and wisdom shine, obstacles will end and blessings mount, all things will be harmonious, and the upper grade of rebirth may be hoped for.

In truth, the way of training has nothing else — only the single word “familiarity.” The great general who splits a willow twig at a hundred paces, the oil seller who pours oil through the hole of a coin — both are “familiarity.” That is to say, “familiarity” is the core of all skills and attainments. The essentials of the formula of “familiarity” come down to three points: first, correct method and steps; second, a great deal of repeated training (from familiarity comes skill, from skill comes wonder, from wonder comes transformation); third, ceaseless pondering, summing up, improving, and raising higher. Follow this, and there is nothing that will not succeed.
[The oil seller who pours oil through the hole of a coin]

“Duke Chen Kangsu (Yaozi) was expert at archery, unequaled in his day, and he prided himself on it. Once, when he was shooting in his family’s archery ground, an oil seller set down his load and stood watching him askance, and for a long time did not leave. Seeing him shoot, hitting eight or nine of ten arrows, the old man merely nodded slightly. Kangsu asked: ‘Do you too understand archery? Is my shooting not superb?’ The old man said: ‘There is nothing to it; it is only that my hand is practiced.’ Kangsu said angrily: ‘How dare you belittle my shooting!’ The old man said: ‘I know it from pouring oil.’ So he took a gourd and set it on the ground, covered its mouth with a coin, and slowly ladled oil and poured it down through the hole of the coin, and the coin was not wet. Then he said: ‘I too have nothing else; it is only that my hand is practiced.’ Kangsu laughed and sent him away.”
(Collected Works of Ouyang Wenzhong · Record of Returning to the Fields)

Translation: Chen Yaozi (the top graduate of the Northern Song, an official up to military commissioner of the Wuxin army, posthumously granted the title Grand Commandant and the posthumous name “Kangsu”) was skilled at archery, unequaled in the world, and he too took pride in it. Once, when he was shooting in the archery ground at home, an old oil seller put down his load, stood at the edge of the ground squinting at him as he shot, and for a long time did not leave. Seeing him hit eight or nine of ten arrows, the old man only nodded slightly. Chen Yaozi asked the old man: “Do you also understand archery? Is my skill at archery not superb?” The old oil seller said: “There is nothing remarkable in it; it is merely that the hand is practiced.” Chen Yaozi said angrily: “How dare you make light of my archery!” The old man said: “By my experience of pouring oil, I can know this principle.” Then he brought out a gourd and placed it on the ground, covered the mouth of the gourd with a copper coin, slowly ladled oil with a spoon and poured it down, so that the oil entered through the hole of the coin, and yet the coin was not moistened. The old man then said: “I too have no other mystery; it is merely that the hand is practiced.” Chen Yaozi could only laugh and send him away.
Q: How does one “ponder, sum up, improve, and raise higher”?

A: First you must have prompt and correct feedback: how did I do in this session of training? Which things were right and which wrong; which reached the expected goal and which did not; how was my state of mind, and how well did I do at self-strengthening, self-discipline, and self-mastery? Then, in light of this, draw up the plan for the next session of training and the goals to be reached, preserving and developing what is good and correcting and improving what is not. In the next session, carry it out according to this plan and these goals. Remember:
Confidence brings success, self-strengthening brings accomplishment, self-discipline brings growth, and self-mastery brings a pure mind.
[Self-strengthening] Rousing oneself to strive for strength. [Self-discipline] Restraining oneself. [Self-mastery] Mastering one’s material desires.

Training is hard, even dry and dull — as the saying goes, “the sharp edge of a sword comes from grinding, and the fragrance of the plum blossom from the bitter cold.” But you can cultivate interest in the midst of training and realization. Once interest has been cultivated, you will take joy in it and enjoy the whole process of training. At that point the work gains power, interest runs high, and you cannot stop — you set your cloud-white sail straight and cross the vast sea.

Therefore the key to study and practice is: make the unfamiliar familiar, and the familiar unfamiliar. The unfamiliar is the mind abiding on the Buddha’s name; the familiar is the mind roving after the five desires and six dusts — a habit formed over beginningless kalpas, and the root of birth and death and the cycle of rebirth.
Master Hanshan teaches in the Dream Journey Collection:

“All that we do in our daily use, every stirring of the mind and movement of thought, is deluded thinking; it is the root of birth and death, and so it invites bitter fruit. Now if one turns the mind of deluded thought into Buddha-recitation, then thought after thought becomes a cause of the Pure Land — this is the fruit of joy. If one recites the Buddha with mind after mind unbroken, deluded thoughts are extinguished, the light of the mind is revealed, wisdom appears, and one accomplishes the Dharma-body of the Buddha.”
“Once Lord Ouyang Wenzhong
(Ouyang Xiu)

asked a monk: ‘When the ancients stood at the brink of birth and death, some took their leave laughing and talking; why is there no one like that now?’ The monk said: ‘The ancients kept thought after thought in samādhi and prajñā, so how could they be confused at the end? People today keep thought after thought in scatteredness, so how could they be settled at the end?’ Wenzhong was greatly startled: ‘These words
(thought after thought in samādhi and prajñā)
are precisely the aim
(goal)

of our study of the Way.’ ... Study of the Way has no other device: what is unfamiliar must be made familiar and what is familiar must be made unfamiliar; when this is done for long and becomes utterly proficient, it merges into one piece, and naturally thought after thought is Amitābha and everywhere is the Pure Land. Lately I see students of the Way who only know to crave the mysterious and wondrous, and do not know to apply dead effort at the root. When they come to the brink of honor and disgrace, calamity and death, then they are all fluster and confusion. This is not others misleading them; they mislead themselves.”

“What is called the root of birth and death is none other than the various deluded thoughts of our daily use — the afflictions and karma of self and others, hate and love, greed, anger, and delusion, and so on. If even a single thread of these is not cut, it is the root of birth and death. Now, if you wish to inquire into Chan and attain sudden enlightenment and be done with birth and death, please weigh it for yourself: can you, in one thought, suddenly cut off the afflictions of many kalpas, as if slicing through tangled silk? If you cannot cut off the afflictions, then even if you can suddenly awaken, it becomes demonic karma — how can this be taken lightly? The sudden awakenings of the patriarchs of the past likewise came out of gradual cultivation accumulated through many lives. Therefore the one matter of sudden awakening is easy to speak of but truly hard; without twenty or thirty years of work in which the mind is utterly dead, how could one, in a single thought amid the heat of affliction, suddenly awaken? The point is whether one knows one’s own capacities. As for the one gate of Buddha-recitation, the world does not know its wonder and regards it as shallow and near at hand; in truth it steps on solid ground at every step. Why? Because since we were born, thought after thought we have deluded and grasped at conditions, creating the karma of birth and death — when have we ever turned the light back for a single thought to illumine our own mind? When have we ever been willing, for a single thought, to cut off afflictions? Now if one can in truth turn the mind of deluded thought into Buddha-recitation, then thought after thought one cuts off afflictions. If thought after thought one can cut off afflictions, then thought after thought one leaves birth and death behind. If this one thought is undisturbed, then at the approach of death evil karma is extinguished, the realm of the Buddha appears before one, and with a single thought one follows the Buddha to rebirth in the Pure Land, forever transcending birth and death and ascending to the stage of non-retrogression. As it is said, ‘Once you see Amitābha, why worry that you will not awaken?’ ... If one can hold to the single thought of Buddha-recitation without shifting, with one mind undisturbed, that is a more certain landing place than Chan inquiry. In sum, it depends only on whether the one thought is genuine. But Chan inquiry requires that the worldly mind be utterly dead, allowing not a single deluded thought. Buddha-recitation uses a pure thought to turn a defiled thought and uses thought to remove thought; it is a method of exchange, and easier given our capacities. In truth, when mind after mind recites the Buddha and mind after mind is undimmed, the wondrous joy of this mind is beyond words.”
“In wearing away habitual tendencies, the power of the thought of recitation must be the mainstay. Whether it be an ancient’s huatou, or simply one mantra held up
(for a Buddha-reciter, it is one phrase of the Buddha’s name)

, hold it firmly in mind and keep it in your thoughts at all times. When over a long time this thought becomes utterly proficient and there is a master at the center, then when you meet conditions and encounter circumstances, within nothing comes out and without nothing enters, and in between
(that is, in the interval)

one thought stands alone, brightly clear. In all dealings with affairs and people, it is like a mirror reflecting forms: it does not welcome, it does not send; when things come it does not stick, when they go there is no trace. This is the first place where you gain power. If subtle feelings and thoughts quietly grow and lengthen unawares, or if you are attached to your own views and understanding, grudging and protecting your sore spot, unwilling to cut it in two at one stroke — then this is where you drift along in softness and warmth, excusing and deceiving yourself. Here
(this)

you must look most intently; you must never let it pass, nor let it fool you. If you lightly let it go and forgive it, that is self-deception. Therefore Confucius said: do not deceive yourself. This is teaching us how to walk the road, taking our hand and helping us along at every step. For our feelings are dim and our wisdom dark; we have always played the clever man in the gateway of light and shadow, in the shadow of the consciousness-spirit, having nothing to do with the true ground of the original place. If you can recognize here, it is like sifting gold from sand. When the sand and earth are gone, the body of gold is pure of itself, and you need not fear that the time of refined radiance will not come.”
Q: How does one become undisturbed at all times?

A: Reciting in units of ten phrases, you may stop counting hundreds and thousands and simply let it be unbroken. Hold it until utterly proficient: “in holding, not holding; in not holding, holding” — when the thought does not move, then it is efficacious. The key point of being undisturbed at all times is: when reciting the Buddha’s name, to know clearly that there are no deluded thoughts — not merely to feel that there are none. The Sutra of Prajñā-Pāramitā Spoken by Mañjuśrī says:
“If a man learns archery, with long practice he becomes skilled; afterwards, though he does not intend it, every arrow he shoots hits the mark.”
When the work of Buddha-recitation is deep, one will of himself arrive at this: the moment the Buddha’s name is raised, deluded thoughts all vanish.
Q: May I use this method from the very beginning to attain being undisturbed at all times?

A: If by using this method you recite more and more purely, then you may. If deluded thoughts are always mixed in when you recite the Buddha’s name and show no sign of diminishing, then you must first achieve being undisturbed through a hundred phrases, then through a thousand phrases, and only then use this method.

Q: The text above says that “the key point of being undisturbed at all times is: when reciting the Buddha’s name, to know clearly that there are no deluded thoughts,” but after many efforts I still have not attained it. Where should I begin?

A: This is because your skill in contemplating the mind is not yet sufficient. You should now strengthen your study of the chapter “Awareness of Thoughts” to raise your power of contemplating the mind, and in particular work hard at the section “Knowing Yet Not Following.” In time you will of course arrive at “when reciting the Buddha’s name, knowing clearly that there are no deluded thoughts.”
Q: I have already achieved being undisturbed through a thousand phrases, and now I am training in being undisturbed at all times: must I recite in units of ten phrases?

A: Everyone’s situation differs; there is no fixed method. “Reciting in units of ten phrases” has a most marked effect and should be used as much as possible. Of course, on certain occasions you may use whatever method you are already accustomed to. For example, while eating, one word per chew; while walking in meditation, one word or two words per step. At this stage it is very helpful to read repeatedly and carefully the Treatise on Buddha-Recitation, the Essentials of Chan and Pure Land, and the Essentials of Buddha-Recitation compiled by the layman Mao Tiyuan. In sum, a method of Buddha-recitation is good if it gathers in the mind, endures, and resists interference, so that mind after mind recites the Buddha and mind after mind is undimmed. If you are fairly sure of being undisturbed at all times, then you may recite phrase by phrase, with a certain interval between phrases and no alien thought.
Q: At this stage, should one recite the Buddha’s name aloud (vocal recitation), silently, or in vajra recitation?

A: Generally speaking, reciting aloud is tiring, and silent recitation easily sinks into dullness, so it is best to make vajra recitation the main practice, interspersed with aloud and silent recitation. But this is only speaking generally. Specifically, it differs from person to person and with the depth of one’s work. If you can recite aloud for a long time and recite silently without dullness, then aloud and silent recitation are no inferior to vajra recitation and have their own distinctive merits. You had best try more yourself and see which method suits which situation better.
[Vajra recitation] When reciting the Buddha’s name, the lips and tongue move but no sound is uttered.
Q: “Thought after thought continuing without interruption” is wonderful. How does one achieve thought after thought continuing without interruption?

A: Once you have achieved being undisturbed through a hundred phrases, you may train in “thought after thought continuing without interruption.” The key point is: take care that between this phrase and the next there is no deluded thought, and recite the next phrase well. Proceeding by degrees in this way, you arrive at thought after thought continuing without interruption. If a deluded thought arises in between, you must be aware of it. Then rouse your spirits, gather your attention, and go on reciting. Master Shandao says:

“It is precisely because invoking the Name is easy that, with continuity, rebirth follows. If one can be unbroken thought after thought, taking the end of life as the limit, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn.

May all people reflect well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, one must spur the mind and restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing. When the former thought ends, the next is born, forever enjoying the bliss of the unconditioned, even up to Buddhahood — is this not joy!”
(See
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching

) There is a vivid simile for “thought after thought continuing without interruption”: on a winter night you hold a flashlight and walk along the ridge between flooded fields; a moment’s carelessness and you will stumble into the water. What should you do? The solution is: always keep the ground beneath your feet lit, and step well the next step. Awareness is the light of the flashlight, always lighting the ground beneath your feet (the space between this phrase and the next, and the next phrase), and you step well the next step (recite the next phrase well).
Q: To be undisturbed at all times, how should one work and live?

A: To put it vividly, the conditions we inhabit can be divided into two worlds: the world of the present moment and the world of the head. The world of the present moment is the condition that your five faculties (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body) contact right now; the world of the head is the condition that exists in your head as you think of this and that. A cultivator should dwell in the world of the present moment at all times and in all places; to fall into the world of the head is to turn one’s back on the Way. On this the patriarchs long ago gave clear instruction. It has been quoted above, but let us quote it again as follows:

A student asked Chan Master Zhaozhou: how should one who has understood the mind and seen the nature conduct himself? Chan Master Zhaozhou replied: he should practice greatly. The student said: I do not know whether a master of your attainment still practices. Chan Master Zhaozhou said: I just wear clothes and eat food. The student said: wearing clothes and eating food are ordinary matters — can this too be practice? Chan Master Zhaozhou said: if it were not practice, then tell me, what do I do every day? (Original text:

“Question: What of the one who has settled the matter? The Master said: He practices greatly. The student said: I wonder whether the monk still practices? The Master said: wearing clothes and eating food. The student said: wearing clothes and eating food are ordinary matters; I wonder whether that is practice? The Master said: You tell me, what do I do every day?”
(Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhaozhou))
Master Hanshan says:

“Someone asked: ‘The ancients ate when hungry and slept when tired, and that was the Way. People today eat when hungry and sleep when tired — why is that not the Way?’ The answer: ‘The ancients, eating, only ate; sleeping, only slept — therefore it was the Way. People today, eating, do not eat; sleeping, do not sleep,
(but instead)

foolishly calculate — therefore they turn their backs on the Way.’ From this we see that in your daily use you need only raise your eyebrows, give a shout, and make spirits start and ghosts fear, make the heavenly demons’ gall break and the dark ghosts’ souls melt, and with one shout drive them all back, leaving the original ground utterly still and quiet, not a thread hanging, bare and naked, clean and pure. Taking this one style of house, when you want to read, then read; when you do not read, toss it aside and do not hang a single word on it. When you want to write, then write; when you do not write, toss it aside and do not foolishly calculate. Even when you drink tea or eat food, just drink tea and eat food; when you want to sleep, then sleep; when you want to relieve yourself, then relieve yourself. Meeting it, it is done, and you must not think about it afterwards. Like a wandering ghost, clean and pure, spotless and white — and you must not sit inside that cleanness and purity
(do not lose awareness and fall into blankness)

. In this way, going straight in with a single blade, with one thought forward, then when you read you meet the ancients face to face, and when you write you spit it out from your own breast in one mouthful, with no before or after. When storing it up is just when you pour it out, and when pouring it out is just when you store it up. In this way you are not turned about by movement and stillness, light and dark, nor shifted by the various devices.”
(Dream Journey Collection · Instruction to Huang Weiheng)

Therefore, at all times, you must never pointlessly fall into the world of the head. Even when working, your thinking should be limited to what the work requires. In dealing with people and affairs, you should give when conditions come and be still when conditions go, and not think about it afterwards. These are principles a cultivator must strictly observe in work and life. But because, since beginningless kalpas, the great majority of the time has been spent rolling about in the world of the head, this deep-rooted bad habit is hard to uproot all at once; you must spend great effort and apply bitter work to grind it away. This is why cultivation is necessary, and this is also where the effort of cultivation must be applied.
Q: Sometimes I clearly know that I am indulging in deluded thinking and want to break free of the world of the head, but I cannot help thinking on. What should I do?

A: You have already entered the stage of “being undisturbed at all times,” which shows that you have considerable power of samādhi and prajñā; you must have full confidence in yourself — it is like learning the sword for ten years deep in the mountains and receiving the true transmission, and now coming out to roam the rivers and lakes. When you are shrouded by deluded thoughts and cannot pull yourself free, then recite a hundred phrases of the Buddha’s name, and another hundred phrases, without stopping, and firmly grasp the key point of “reciting and contemplating at once.” If you recite more and more purely and finally enter the state of one mind undisturbed, that is very good. If you cannot enter it, do not be discouraged: so long as you firmly grasp the key point of “reciting and contemplating at once,” your power is growing — and growing in actual combat. Persist day after day, and you will certainly defeat the deluded thoughts.

There is another method: when you truly cannot help thinking on, do not forbid it; instead, carefully observe this thinker and see what exactly he wants to do. It is like sitting down to watch a play: since this thinker wants to perform, very well, let him perform — see what he plays — but you must be sure to see clearly what he is playing. This is most interesting; watch the performance in this way often, and firmly grasp the key point of “seeing clearly.” Unawares, one day you will find that when a deluded thought is about to arise, you give yourself the command: do not think. And the deluded thought stops at once — clear and still, wonderful beyond words. At that time you will be able to do this: the moment a deluded thought arises, replace it at once with the Buddha’s name, and abide in the state of one mind undisturbed. What remains is to consolidate and deepen this samādhi. Samādhi means: within, not turned about by deluded thoughts; without, not dragged along by conditions.
Q: How does one utterly kill the thieving mind?
A: The thieving mind is deluded thought (the feelings of consciousness). To utterly kill the thieving mind is to cut off deluded thoughts utterly — whoever comes, cut him down! Master Hanshan says:
“As for the one gate of Buddha-recitation, the world does not know its wonder and regards it as shallow and near at hand,
(wonderful!)

yet in truth it steps on solid ground at every step. Why? Because since we were born, thought after thought we have deluded and grasped at conditions, creating the karma of birth and death — when have we ever turned the light back for a single thought to illumine our own mind? When have we ever been willing, for a single thought, to cut off afflictions? Now if one can in truth turn the mind of deluded thought into Buddha-recitation, then thought after thought one cuts off afflictions. If thought after thought one can cut off afflictions, then thought after thought one leaves birth and death behind. If this one thought is undisturbed
(the key!)

, then at the approach of death evil karma is extinguished, the realm of the Buddha appears before one, and with a single thought one follows the Buddha to rebirth in the Pure Land, forever transcending birth and death and ascending to the stage of non-retrogression.”
(Dream Journey Collection · Reply to Wang Yufan)
[The thieving mind] Master Zhongfeng says:
“What is a thieving mind? It is another name for the feelings of consciousness, because it can rob one of one’s own supreme Dharma-treasure.”
(Zhongfeng’s Extensive Record · Night Talks in the Mountain Hut)
Master Lianchi says:

“Birth and death do not depart from a single thought; indeed, all dharmas of the world and beyond do not depart from a single thought. Now if one recites the Buddha with this very thought, how intimate and essential it is! If you can see through where this thought arises, that is the Amitābha of one’s own nature, that is the patriarchs’ coming from the West. Even if you do not awaken, riding the power of this thought you will be reborn in Ultimate Bliss, and there you will cut birth and death across the board, escape the cycle of rebirth, and in the end greatly awaken. I pray you let go of the myriad conditions, and throughout the twelve hours keep this thought alert and awake — this is my utmost hope!”
(Collected Works of Yunqi)
[Alert and awake] To stay wakeful and roused, maintaining right mindfulness. The Gateless Barrier of the Chan School says:
“Take the three hundred and sixty bones and joints and the eighty-four thousand pores, and raise a mass of doubt through the whole body, investigating the word ‘wu,’ alert and awake day and night.”
The Complete Works of Zhu Xi
Preserving and Nurturing says: “Only keep yourself always alert and awake; accumulate little by little, and after a long time it will of course continue and merge into one piece.”
Master Hanshan says:

“As for the one gate of the Pure Land, it draws in living beings and its benefit is the widest; through the ages very many who recited the Buddha have attained rebirth. But the essential thing is single-minded devotion — it is not a matter of one or two gatherings a month, reciting the Buddha’s name a few thousand times, and taking that as the main practice. First of all you must give rise to the vow, deeply weary of saṃsāra as suffering, resolved to renounce it, and fixing your thoughts on the Western Pure Land, on being born by transformation in the lotus, thinking thought after thought that you must be reborn in that land and see Amitābha face to face — take this as your original vow. Each day, morning and evening, you must set fixed lessons: whether holding the Diamond Sutra, or holding the Amitābha Sutra, or holding the Rebirth Mantra, you must recite the Buddha and dedicate the merit toward the West, vowing to be reborn there, and take this as your fixed rule. Throughout the six periods of the day, whether at leisure or busy, in movement or stillness, hold the one phrase Amitābha Buddha in your mind, never forgetting it, mind after mind unbroken, until even in sleep and dreams you do not forget it. When it becomes one piece in this way, with no gap
(in ancient usage, the same as “interval”)

unbroken, it is called one-practice samādhi. When this thought is utterly proficient, no circumstance or condition can interrupt it; eyes open or eyes closed, the one phrase Amitābha Buddha stands clearly before you. All the worldly entanglements — parents, wife and children, the various deluded thoughts of love and desire and the thoughts of karma — are worn away and purified by the one phrase of the Buddha’s name, and in this way your own mind becomes pure. The sutra says: ‘When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.’ Reciting the Buddha and applying the mind in this way, when you reach the moment of death there is only the one phrase Amitābha Buddha before you, one mind undisturbed, and you will naturally see Amitābha Buddha come in person to receive and guide you. In the space of a single thought you attain rebirth in the Pure Land; from then on you forever escape the suffering of birth and death, ascend to Ultimate Bliss, and are born by transformation in the lotus — this is the proof of a lifetime of Buddha-recitation. If one is so single-minded and devoted and yet is not reborn, then all the Buddhas would be guilty of lying. But if the years pass idly, with the mouth speaking of Buddha-recitation and the mind without actual practice, that is hiding from and deceiving oneself — when would there ever be a time of proof? Good men, since you have given rise to faith, you should practice in earnest; never deceive yourselves.”
(Dream Journey Collection
Instruction to the Assembly of Practitioners at Yihua)
Q: I am resolved to go all out in Buddha-recitation. Where should I begin?

A: Set rules for yourself: (by day) the moment your business is finished, recite the Buddha’s name at once; (by night) as long as you have not fallen asleep, recite the Buddha’s name without stopping. To ensure the quality of your Buddha-recitation, you may use the method of reciting in sections: divide the day into sections according to units of activity, and then recite the Buddha’s name section by section. You must have a clear idea of how each section was recited, so that you can make targeted improvements. For example, rising and dressing is one section, making the bed is one section, going to the washroom is one section, brushing the teeth and washing the face is one section, one meal is one section, and so on. Or again, when walking outdoors, take the tree or signboard ahead as the end point of the present section, and fix a distance as one section; when that section is walked, fix the next section, and so on. Or again, on a bus, each stop is one section. At the beginning, you may make each section shorter according to your own situation; as the work deepens, gradually lengthen each section. In sum, manage it flexibly yourself and seek real effect. In every section you must strive to achieve:
one mind undisturbed in Buddha-recitation.
Form it into a fixed rule, persevere without letting up, and as days pass and the work deepens, practice becomes second nature. In this way the upper grade of rebirth may be hoped for.

As for how to recite the Buddha’s name well, fellow practitioners should communicate more and encourage one another more; treat others as yourself, and in saving others you save yourself; pool wisdom and form a team. Good experiences in Buddha-recitation should also be published and shared online, so that all hearts are of one mind and together we run toward Ultimate Bliss.
Q: When I recite the Buddha’s name while eating, I recite one word per chew. This has reduced my deluded thoughts a great deal, but they are not wholly gone. What should I do?

A: The work must be carried out step by step. You may recite in this way: one word per chew, and count once every three phrases of the Buddha’s name, from one to ten; then from one to ten again; and so continue. Each time you count, note whether there are deluded thoughts. This method can be extended to the many situations in daily life where one word accompanies one movement, and it is very effective. Of course, numbers are only a walking stick; when the mind’s thought has become concentrated to a certain degree, you may throw it away, and be one mind undisturbed without a walking stick.
Q: Must one count how many phrases of the Buddha’s name one recites each day?

A: The purpose of counting is to urge oneself not to become lazy, and to have a clear idea of how much one recites each day and whether one is diligent or slack. If you are already able to keep it up without laziness, you may stop counting. Master Yungu (Master Hanshan’s teacher) says:
“You
(referring to Mr. Liaofan)

are not yet able to be without mind, but you can hold the Cundi mantra. Without noting or counting, let it not be interrupted; hold it until utterly proficient: in holding, not holding; in not holding, holding — when the thought does not move, then it is efficacious.”
(See Liao Fan’s Four Lessons) Although this teaching speaks of how to hold a mantra, it has much to inspire in the holding of the Name as well.

[Without counting or noting] Not counting. [In holding, not holding] When reciting the mantra one is so utterly sincere and focused that one no longer knows that one is reciting. [In not holding, holding] When not reciting, one is still reciting subconsciously. This is what Buddha-reciters often call the state of “reciting yet without recitation, not reciting yet reciting.” [When the thought does not move] To realize the state of no-thought and yet not no-thought.
As for the states of mantra-holding, Master Huiming set out the three gates of mantra-holding:
“What is the first gate? The student holds and recites the true words
(mantra)

, holding until ten thousand thoughts return to one and no second thought arises; this is called penetrating the first gate. But this is still pressing down grass with a stone, and is not yet ultimate. What is the second gate? When the true words are held to the point of holding yet not holding, not holding yet holding, and who it is that holds even oneself does not know, and it is even as if two people were holding it together — this is called samādhi manifesting, and is also called penetrating the second gate. What is the third gate? When the true words are held to the point where true, false, and Dharma are all three unknown, and one enters deeply into samādhi, attaining the right concentration beyond holding, with nothing whatsoever, and thus realizes the true aspect, complete in all things — this is called penetrating the three gates.”
Record of Master Huiming’s Teachings

blocks.text: Chapter Eight: Purifying the Mind and Gathering Merit

inline.s: The Buddha said: “One cannot be reborn in that land through few roots of goodness, blessings, and causes.”

Afflictions are thousands upon thousands; summed up, they are the three poisons: greed, anger, and delusion. When the work of Buddha-recitation gains power, you must use the Buddha’s name to subdue afflictions,
purify your mind-ground and store up provisions for rebirth
. The ancients said:
“When a practitioner’s pure karma has ripened and his mind-ground is pure, he accords with the Buddha, and only then does he see the Buddha appear before him and receive him to be born in the West.”

The Buddha’s moon is in the sky, its light shining upon the water of a million minds. If the mind is not pure, it is like water stirred and turbid: though the moon is in the sky, its reflection does not appear. Therefore, when one whose thoughts are in disorder at the moment of death is received by the Buddha’s radiance, he is like a blind man who cannot see it.

[The three poisons] Poison means what harms. Greed, anger, and delusion harm the supramundane mind of goodness, and so they are called poisons. First, the poison of greed: the mind that draws in and takes is called greed. If with a deluded mind one meets any agreeable condition and takes delight in drawing it in, this is called the poison of greed. Second, the poison of anger: the mind of hatred is called anger. If with a deluded mind one meets any disagreeable condition and is displeased and repelled by it, this is called the poison of anger. Third, the poison of delusion: the mind of confusion is called delusion. If regarding all matters and principles one understands nothing, and takes them up perversely and falsely, giving rise to wrong actions, this is called the poison of delusion.

Among the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion, greed is the root; anger and delusion both arise from greed. Because one cannot get what one craves, or loses what one craves, anger arises; because of craving, one goes against principle,
takes things up perversely and falsely,
and so delusion arises. Therefore, to extinguish afflictions, one must work at cutting off craving. The Buddha said:
“To be free of desire and still is the most supreme.”
(Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters)

Ordinary people cannot be without thought: if they do not think of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they will certainly think of greed, anger, and delusion. Thinking of greed, anger, and delusion, the evil karma of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct swarms up, and the cycle of birth and death never ceases. The Buddha therefore guided them according to their inclination, seizing on the habit by which living beings cannot be without thought, and with skillful means used one Buddha-thought to replace deluded thoughts, so that living beings turn deluded thoughts into Buddha-thought and exchange the defiled mind for the pure mind, and thus easily attain rebirth in the Pure Land and escape birth and death. Master Chewu says:

“The essentials of purifying the mind are likewise nothing but Buddha-recitation. One thought in accord, one thought a Buddha; thought after thought in accord, thought after thought a Buddha. When the clear pearl
(the precious pearl that clarifies muddy water)
is dropped into muddy water, the muddy water cannot but become clear; when the Buddha’s name is cast into a confused mind, the confused mind cannot but become Buddha.”

(Collected Writings of Master Chewu) Therefore Buddha-recitation is the most intimate and simplest transformation, made at the place where living beings’ birth and death is closest to them. And the key to making this transformation is awareness: awareness in every thought, so that the moment a deluded thought arises, it is at once turned away with the Buddha’s name.
You must earnestly and truly do the work of “awareness
turning away,” not letting a single thought slip past, seeing through every thought.
As days pass and the work deepens, it will of course merge into one piece, subdue the afflictions, and accomplish pure karma. The key to purifying the mind is simply this:
use the Buddha’s name to turn deluded thoughts away.

[Not letting a single thought slip past] Do not let any deluded thought slip by (do not be fooled by it). [Seeing through every thought] Do not be shrouded by any deluded thought; do not listen to it or let it make sport of you; do not take it as something real.
To be done with birth and death, you must know the root of birth and death and how to uproot it. The patriarchs taught:
The root of birth and death is the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion, and to uproot the root of birth and death is to spare no effort in the single thought of turning this mind!

In the conditions that appear before you in daily use — when wife and children gather, when relatives and friends meet, where righteousness and profit, adversity and favor press from both sides, before joy and anger, greed and hatred have arisen — you must fix your gaze in advance, truly and clearly, see what the root of birth and death is, and immediately uproot it with all your strength.
All suffering arises from craving; therefore the way to end suffering is: wherever craving arises, there uproot it and extinguish it.

[All suffering arises from craving] Craving accumulates suffering (craving creates suffering); it is the root of suffering. Because of craving, there is grasping; because of grasping, there is karma; because of karma, there is suffering; because of suffering, there is the cycle of rebirth. Craving arises where the six faculties (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind) meet the six dusts (forms, sounds, scents, tastes, touches, and dharmas); therefore you must guard the gates of the six faculties closely, and the moment a dust is contacted, illumine it and cut off the root of delusion — this is the key.
The Buddha said:

“Monks, what is the noble truth of the arising of suffering? It is craving, which leads to renewed existence, is bound up with delight and lust, and seeks pleasure here and there — namely, craving for sense-desires, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. And where does this craving arise and take its stand? In the world of body and mind, wherever there is anything enticing and delightful, there craving arises and takes its stand. And in the world of body and mind, what is enticing and delightful? In the world of body and mind, the eye faculty is enticing and delightful; there craving arises and takes its stand. In the world of body and mind, the ear faculty is enticing and delightful; there craving arises and takes its stand. ... Again, monks, what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving, its abandoning, its relinquishing, its release, its freedom from attachment. But, monks, where is craving to be uprooted, where extinguished? In the world of body and mind, wherever there is anything enticing and delightful — there craving is to be uprooted and extinguished. And in the world of body and mind, what is enticing and delightful? In the world of body and mind, the eye faculty is enticing and delightful; there craving is uprooted and extinguished. In the world of body and mind, the ear faculty is enticing and delightful; there craving is uprooted and extinguished. ...”
(See
Commentary on the Great Sutta on the Foundations of Mindfulness

[Truth] The real and unerring principle. [The four noble truths] The truth of suffering, the truth of accumulation, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path. First, the “truth of suffering” is the truth that explains that life is full of suffering. Suffering has the mark of oppression; suffering is the reality of actual life. Second, the “truth of accumulation”: “accumulation” means to bring about, to cause; it is the truth that explains how the suffering of life comes about. The pain of life is due to craving, and so there is grasping, and so there is karma, and so there is suffering, and so there is the cycle of rebirth. Third, the “truth of cessation” is the truth that explains the extinguishing of all suffering. When all the accumulation of suffering (craving) is forever cut off without remainder, with no grasping and no attachment, then there is no more karma, no more suffering, no more cycle of rebirth — this is the truth of cessation. Fourth, the “truth of the path” explains how to forever cut off the accumulation of suffering (craving), that is, the way to end suffering. Among the four noble truths, accumulation is the cause and suffering the fruit; the path is the cause and cessation the fruit.
The goal of cultivation is to subdue and cut off afflictions; the goal of Confucianism is to perfect benevolence. Its methods of practice are well worth learning from. The Analects
Yan Yuan records:

“Yan Yuan asked about benevolence. The Master said: ‘To master oneself and return to propriety is benevolence. If for a single day one masters oneself and returns to propriety, the whole world will return to benevolence. Benevolence proceeds from oneself — how could it come from others?’ Yan Yuan said: ‘May I ask the particulars?’ The Master said: ‘Look not at what is contrary to propriety; listen not to what is contrary to propriety; speak not what is contrary to propriety; make no movement that is contrary to propriety.’ Yan Yuan said: ‘Though I am not quick, I beg to put these words into practice.’”

(Translation: Once Confucius’s disciple Yan Hui asked how one might attain the state of benevolence. Confucius replied: restrain yourself and make your conduct accord with propriety. If one day you truly achieve this — following your heart’s desire without overstepping the rule — then all under heaven will acknowledge that you have attained benevolence. Attaining benevolence rests entirely with yourself, not on others. Yan Hui asked again: then what concretely should one do? Confucius answered: what is contrary to propriety, do not look at, do not listen to, do not speak of, do not do. Hearing this, Yan Hui said to his teacher: though I am not clever enough, I am resolved to act according to the Master’s words.)
[To master oneself] To restrain oneself. [To return to propriety] To restore the state in which the nature is originally good. [Propriety] A standard of conduct.
Imitating this, there follows the dialogue below:
Q: How does one subdue and cut off afflictions?

A: Master oneself and remove the poisons. Restrain yourself and remove the three poisons (greed, anger, and delusion). If one day you truly achieve following your heart at ease without greed, without anger, without delusion, then all under heaven will acknowledge that you have cut off the afflictions. Cutting off afflictions rests entirely with yourself, not on others.
Q: Then what concretely should one do?

A: Look not at what is contrary to propriety, listen not to what is contrary to propriety, speak not what is contrary to propriety, make no movement contrary to propriety, and think no thought contrary to propriety. Here “propriety” is the standard for body, mouth, and mind: no greed, no anger, no delusion. What is “contrary to propriety” is greed, anger, and delusion. These “five don’ts” mean: the things that make you give rise to greed, anger, and delusion — do not look at them, do not listen to them, do not speak of them, do not do them, do not think of them.

Therefore, to master oneself and remove the poisons: look not at what is contrary to propriety, listen not to what is contrary to propriety, speak not what is contrary to propriety, make no movement contrary to propriety, think no thought contrary to propriety, and do not give rise to a mind dwelling on forms, sounds, scents, tastes, touches, or dharmas — in this way hold down the afflictions and keep them from coming into activity.
In his Preface to Liao Fan’s Four Lessons, Master Yinguang gave a most penetrating teaching on countering afflictions. It is excerpted and annotated below:

“Yet to become a sage is not difficult; it lies in making bright one’s own bright virtue. If you wish to make bright your bright virtue, you must begin with the investigation of things and the extension of knowledge. If the things of human desire cannot be vigorously removed, then the true knowledge that is originally ours can hardly be brought to full manifestation.”

Yet to become a sage is not difficult; it lies only in making manifest the bright and upright virtue of one’s own nature. To make manifest the bright and upright virtue of one’s own nature, one must begin with “removing the things of human desire and manifesting the true knowledge originally present in one’s own mind.” If the things of human desire cannot be vigorously removed, then the true knowledge that is originally ours can hardly be brought to full manifestation.

[Bright virtue] The bright and upright virtue of one’s own nature. This is what everyone inherently possesses, but it is locked away and obscured by all kinds of unreasonable feelings and thoughts, and so does not appear. [The investigation of things and the extension of knowledge] To remove the things of human desire and manifest the true knowledge originally present in one’s own mind. The Book of Rites
The Great Learning says: “The extension of knowledge lies in the investigation of things; when things are investigated, knowledge is complete.”

“If you wish to make true knowledge manifest, you should, in your daily speech and action, constantly raise awareness and illumination. Do not let any unreasonable feelings and thoughts sprout in the mind even for a moment. Constantly keep the mind empty, bright, and penetrating. Like a mirror set on its stand, it reflects whatever condition appears before it; it only reflects the condition before it and is not turned about by it. Beautiful or ugly is its own affair — what has it to do with me? It does not anticipate what comes, nor cling to what goes.”

If you wish to make true knowledge manifest, then in your daily use, whenever a thought stirs or words and deeds are produced, you should constantly raise awareness and illumination. Do not let any feeling or thought contrary to principle sprout in the mind even briefly. Constantly keep the mind empty, bright, and penetrating, like a bright mirror set on its stand: whatever is before it, it simply reflects it, without being dragged about by it. Whether it is beautiful or ugly is its own affair — what has it to do with me? When it comes, there is no expectation or waiting; when it goes, there is no affliction or clinging.
These few sentences are the key to cultivating the mind: let the true mind be master.

[Speech and action] Words and deeds. [Awareness and illumination] To know clearly what one’s present thought and emotion are. This is the basic skill of turning evil into good, delusion into awakening, and the ordinary into the sage. Hence the patriarchs and great masters often said: at all times and in all places, whatever karma one creates through body, mouth, and mind, one should all the while look back and know this mind. [Yan] Beautiful. [Chi
chī
] Ugly. [Anticipate] That is, “expect beforehand.”

“If unreasonable feelings and thoughts should stir even slightly, you should at once attack and govern them strictly, and wipe them out completely. It is like facing an enemy army: not only must you not let them invade your borders, you must also behead their generals and seize their banners, and wipe out the remaining bandits.”

If unreasonable feelings and thoughts have just begun to appear, you should at once attack and govern them strictly, and wipe them out completely. It is like facing an enemy army: not only must you not let them invade your territory, you must also behead their generals and seize their banners, wipe out the remaining bandits, and root them out entirely.
[Sprouting] Just beginning to appear. [Borders] A region handed over to an official to administer with full authority. [Qian
qiān
] To seize.
